news.title: Pentagon quizzes NATO allies on political loyalty, documents reveal  - Haiti Gazette – Daily Haiti News
news.text:
The Pentagon has handed NATO allies of the United States a long list of questions about whether they are adhering to President Donald Trump’s vision for the transatlantic alliance, according to documents obtained exclusively by Al Jazeera.

The questionnaire asks pointedly whether the allies have been “publicly supportive of US foreign policy priorities”.

Another bullet point poses the query, “Has the country shown alignment with the US approach to [be] ‘strong, clear, and quiet?'” a reference to a phrase used by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in his address at the Shangri-La Dialogue in May.

The markings on the document and the phrasing suggest the questions are meant to guide interactions between US officials and their NATO counterparts during an ongoing six-month Pentagon review of American forces in Europe.

The three-page document, titled “Questions for NATO Allies & Other Key Stakeholders”, was obtained from an official who received it. Bloomberg News first reported on parts of the questionnaire.

The most overtly political questions come at the end. One question probes allies about whether they have placed restrictions on US access to bases and military flights over their countries, an issue that has become a source of friction amid the US-Israel war on Iran.

Several European countries imposed such restrictions after the start of the war on February 28.

“Are they willing to reduce or eliminate any such restrictions?” the questionnaire then asks.

Experts say the document reflects a growing effort under Trump to involve US allies in the Iran war, even if the conflict falls outside the purview of NATO’s collective defence pact.

“This administration has been confusing NATO topics with unilateral US military operations,” a senior defence official from a NATO ally said on condition of anonymity. “This questionnaire also reflects this confusion. NATO has nothing to do with the Middle East.”

The questionnaire asks whether allies have endorsed the Trump administration’s “NATO 3.0” concept, which calls for European allies to take on more responsibility for their own defence with “more limited US support”.

Other lines echo Trump’s demands that the allies spend more on defence and contribute more to NATO’s command and makeup of forces.

Certain countries have already run afoul of the demands the questionnaire refers to.

Trump, for instance, has repeatedly berated Spain over its decision to seek an exemption from a 2025 agreement among NATO allies to raise their military spending to 5 percent of their gross domestic products (GDPs).

Back in March, Spain also closed its airspace to US planes and refused to let the US use bases for attacks against Iran. Trump responded by threatening to cut trade with Madrid.

A senior European official, speaking on condition of anonymity, noted that the questionnaire “doesn’t explicitly condition US military presence on political loyalty”.

But, the official added, it does reflect “the Pentagon’s desire to develop the case for specific, almost vindictive force presence reductions”. It also sends a message to allies to “be on the good side of the White House by expecting close alignment with the White House agenda”.

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to questions about this story.

“These kinds of issues do come up in the conversation, Democrat or Republican,” US former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense Jim Townsend told Al Jazeera’s This is America programme.

“We do know this administration cares very much about loyalty, whether it’s their own people or the allies, particularly. And, you know, he – President Trump – has talked to the allies quite sternly about his expectations for their loyalty and support for the US.”

news.text:

US President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon on Monday to “substantially reduce” the “costly” drills, describing them as a “totally inappropriate and hostile” signal to North Korea while citing his “very good relationship” with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.
The allies had initially planned for the UFS exercise, which began on Monday, to run until August 27. The second phase was reportedly set to include a simulated counteroffensive against North Korea, including the encirclement of its capital.

But the exercise will now end on Friday – marking the first time a theatre-level US-South Korea exercise has been cut short or scaled back while already under way.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff confirmed the change in statement on Wednesday, adding that “the US and South Korea have agreed to discuss and implement various measures to achieve the objectives of the UFS exercise and establish a robust combined defence posture”.

Details about precisely which exercises will be cut remain under discussion.

Analysts warned that cancelling the drills could send the wrong signal to Pyongyang while also setting back Seoul’s efforts to build nuclear-powered submarines with US support and reclaim full control of its military from Washington.
The US has held wartime operational control (Opcon) over South Korea’s military since the outbreak of the Korean war in 1950. Peacetime Opcon was returned in 1994, but the American general who leads the joint Combined Forces Command retains wartime control.

The reduction follows on the heels of Trump’s complaints about South Korea’s refusal to provide material support for the US-Israel war on Iran.

Doo said the move could “delay the process of determining when wartime operational control will be transferred”.
The two countries had previously agreed to conduct a full-scale operational capability assessment of South Korea’s readiness to retake Opcon as part of this year’s drills, with the results due in November.
“Aside from the Opcon transfer issue, it could also weaken the combined defence posture by reducing the frequency of future deployments of US strategic assets to South Korea,” Doo said.
Not only that, but he said the move could undermine South Korea’s central role “in efforts to advance dialogue and improve relations” with the North.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has said Trump should act as the “peacemaker” in negotiations with North Korea, while Seoul assists as a “pacemaker” – setting the tempo for resuming dialogue and easing tensions on the peninsula.
Lee is also pushing to reclaim Opcon from the US before his term ends in 2030.
Some observers expect the scaling back of this year’s UFS to set a precedent, creating a new benchmark for determining the size and composition of future US-South Korea joint exercises.
There are also concerns that Trump might link it to other bilateral issues, including South Korea’s investments in the US, further fuelling what some describe as the “economisation of security”.
Trump was likely expecting South Korea, as an ally, to play a certain role in the war in Iran
Shin Jong-woo, Korea Defence and Security Forum
Shin Jong-woo, secretary general of the Korea Defence and Security Forum, said the motivation for Trump’s decision appeared to be linked to Seoul’s refusal to get involved in the Iran war.
“Trump was likely expecting South Korea, as an ally, to play a certain role in the war in Iran and the issue of the Strait of Hormuz,” Shin said. “Given that President Trump views alliances from a transactional perspective, it is difficult to rule out the possibility that the issue of joint exercises could become linked to other security and economic matters.”
Yoo Ji-hoon, a research fellow at the Korea Institute for Defence Analyses, urged the US and South Korea to maintain a credible combined defence posture, describing joint drills “a mechanism for demonstrating the alliance’s deterrence capability and durability”.
“It is important to adjust them without undermining their fundamental purpose,” he said.

Some have suggested that Trump scaled back the drills as an attempt to pave the way for another summit with Kim, but Professor Yang Moo-jin of the University of North Korean Studies said that any such meeting would likely “end in political stagecraft”, citing Pyongyang’s rejection of denuclearisation and demand to be recognised as a nuclear-armed state.
“This is a bad look all around,” said Jenny Town, a senior fellow at the US-based Stimson Centre think tank.
“Nothing like hanging an ally out to dry for all the world to see,” she wrote on social media. “How are US other allies reading this situation?”

news.title: Pentagon quizzes NATO allies on political loyalty, documents reveal  - St. Vincent Tribune – Daily St
news.text:
The Pentagon has handed NATO allies of the United States a long list of questions about whether they are adhering to President Donald Trump’s vision for the transatlantic alliance, according to documents obtained exclusively by Al Jazeera.

The questionnaire asks pointedly whether the allies have been “publicly supportive of US foreign policy priorities”.

Another bullet point poses the query, “Has the country shown alignment with the US approach to [be] ‘strong, clear, and quiet?'” a reference to a phrase used by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in his address at the Shangri-La Dialogue in May.

The markings on the document and the phrasing suggest the questions are meant to guide interactions between US officials and their NATO counterparts during an ongoing six-month Pentagon review of American forces in Europe.

The three-page document, titled “Questions for NATO Allies & Other Key Stakeholders”, was obtained from an official who received it. Bloomberg News first reported on parts of the questionnaire.

The most overtly political questions come at the end. One question probes allies about whether they have placed restrictions on US access to bases and military flights over their countries, an issue that has become a source of friction amid the US-Israel war on Iran.

Several European countries imposed such restrictions after the start of the war on February 28.

“Are they willing to reduce or eliminate any such restrictions?” the questionnaire then asks.

Experts say the document reflects a growing effort under Trump to involve US allies in the Iran war, even if the conflict falls outside the purview of NATO’s collective defence pact.

“This administration has been confusing NATO topics with unilateral US military operations,” a senior defence official from a NATO ally said on condition of anonymity. “This questionnaire also reflects this confusion. NATO has nothing to do with the Middle East.”

The questionnaire asks whether allies have endorsed the Trump administration’s “NATO 3.0” concept, which calls for European allies to take on more responsibility for their own defence with “more limited US support”.

Other lines echo Trump’s demands that the allies spend more on defence and contribute more to NATO’s command and makeup of forces.

Certain countries have already run afoul of the demands the questionnaire refers to.

Trump, for instance, has repeatedly berated Spain over its decision to seek an exemption from a 2025 agreement among NATO allies to raise their military spending to 5 percent of their gross domestic products (GDPs).

Back in March, Spain also closed its airspace to US planes and refused to let the US use bases for attacks against Iran. Trump responded by threatening to cut trade with Madrid.

A senior European official, speaking on condition of anonymity, noted that the questionnaire “doesn’t explicitly condition US military presence on political loyalty”.

But, the official added, it does reflect “the Pentagon’s desire to develop the case for specific, almost vindictive force presence reductions”. It also sends a message to allies to “be on the good side of the White House by expecting close alignment with the White House agenda”.

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to questions about this story.

“These kinds of issues do come up in the conversation, Democrat or Republican,” US former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense Jim Townsend told Al Jazeera’s This is America programme.

“We do know this administration cares very much about loyalty, whether it’s their own people or the allies, particularly. And, you know, he – President Trump – has talked to the allies quite sternly about his expectations for their loyalty and support for the US.”
